newsitem.title: USA: Depression linked to bone loss - study.
newsitem.headline: Depression linked to bone loss - study.

text.p: Depression may increase a woman's risk of broken bones, a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine suggested.

Medical researchers have uncovered a link between depression and the bone-consuming disease osteoporosis and have calculated that a third of the women who had experienced major depression had bones as brittle as an older person.

The findings suggest that "the lifetime risk of fracture related to depression is substantial," according to a team led by Dr. David Michelson of the National Institute of Mental Health in Bethesda, Maryland.

Their study, which compared 24 women who had suffered from depression at some point in their lives with 24 who had not, found that the bone density of women with a history of depression was as much as 13.6 percent lower, depending on which bones were measured.

Since major depression affects 5 to 9 percent of women and a 10 percent decline in the density of the bones can lead to a 40 percent increase in hip fractures, the discovery of a link between depression and osteoporosis has important public health implications.

"The affected women in this study, average age 41, had bone loss equivalent to that of 70-year-old women. More than a third faced a markedly increased risk of fracture," said Dr. Philip Gold, chief of the NIMH branch where the research was conducted.

The reason bones become more brittle in women who have experienced a serious bout of depression is unclear. Drugs that treat depression may have an effect on the bones, or there may be some element of the mental illness itself that interferes with the growth of bones.

Depression is known to affect the physical body, such as reducing the amount of growth hormone. It can also produce other hormone or nutrition problems. Hormones, particularly estrogen, can affect the rate of bone growth and destruction.
Other studies have shown that people who have suffered from schizophrenia and other mental disorders also have weaker bones.

The Michelson group said that although anti-depression drugs may be weakening the bones, their study did not support such a link. The women who had taken depression-fighting drugs the longest did not tend to have the brittlest bones.
But they cautioned women in the study may have recalled inaccurately how much anti-depression medicine they had taken.
